one_liner: Scheme-to-C compiler and runtime whose executables run about 2x faster than Guile 3.0.11 on the R7RS benchmark suite.
what_it_does: Gambit is a full Scheme system: gsc compiles Scheme (R7RS plus many SRFIs and Gambit extensions) through its Gambit Virtual Machine (GVM) intermediate form to C and then to a native executable (gsc -exe) or loadable module, and gsi is the interpreter and REPL. A JavaScript target (-target js) exists alongside C. It is not a drop-in for Guile: programs are compiled ahead of time, and Guile modules, GOOPS and Guile-specific APIs do not carry over, though portable R7RS code compiles with little change.
how_it_is_fast: Whole-module compilation to C with --enable-single-host, which emits each Scheme module as a single C function; INSTALL.txt says this roughly doubles interpreter speed, and that GCC's computed gotos cut execution time by about 35%. With (standard-bindings), (extended-bindings) and (block) declarations the compiler can inline primitives such as + and car and treat file-local definitions as constants; proper tail calls are kept without relying on C TCO. Floating-point code is strong: in the suite Gambit beats even Chez on fft (2.6x), mbrot (1.7x) and pnpoly (1.4x) (derived from page data).
when_to_use: AOT-compiled Scheme programs where Guile, Chicken, Cyclone, Larceny or Racket is the current choice and throughput matters: in ecraven/r7rs-benchmarks Gambit 4.9.7 is about 1.95x faster than Guile 3.0.11 (median 1.95x), 2.7x faster than Chicken 5.4.0 and 1.45x faster than Racket 9.0 by geomean (derived from page data)
Floating-point-heavy kernels (fft, mbrot, nucleic, ray, simplex, pnpoly), where Gambit is 3-5.6x faster than Guile and also ahead of Chez 10.3.0
Code using call/cc or deep continuations (ctak 23x and fibc 17x faster than Guile)
Shipping a standalone native executable or embedding Scheme in a C program, or targeting JavaScript from the same source
As the base for Gerbil Scheme, which runs on Gambit
when_not_to_use: When raw speed is the only criterion and Chez Scheme is an option: Chez is faster on aggregate (Gambit geomean about 0.79x of Chez speed, faster on 17 of 54 rows), and much faster on gcbench (9x), graphs (4.6x) and ctak/fibc (about 4x)
Bignum-heavy work: no GMP integration (issue #761, open bounty, reports about a 100x fixnum-to-bignum gap); pi and chudnovsky run 7.1x and 2.9x slower than Guile
String-building and allocation-heavy GC workloads: string:500000:100 is 15.6x slower than Guile (3.20 s vs 0.20 s, about the same as Chez) and gcbench 5.6x slower
Multicore parallelism: the manual says Scheme threads are managed by Gambit's runtime, not OS threads, and at most one runs at a time (an --enable-smp configure option exists but is not the default)

Very large single source files: the suite's compiler.scm failed because gcc's cc1 was killed while compiling the generated C (COMPILEERROR), and INSTALL.txt warns single-host builds with --enable-gcc-opts take about 2 GB and over 10 minutes

integration.dependencies: a C compiler (GCC strongly recommended for computed gotos; clang works); OpenSSL optional
integration.min_toolchain: GCC 3.3 or later recommended by INSTALL.txt; any C99-era compiler for the generated C
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS and Windows (CI badge), portable C output for other Unix-likes; JavaScript target via -target js
integration.thread_safety: Green (runtime-managed) SRFI-18/21 threads, at most one running per VM; hash tables are not safe for concurrent modification by Gambit threads (issue #322, open)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — portable R7RS programs compile with gsc, but Guile modules, GOOPS, Guile's FFI and its JIT/REPL workflow do not carry over

gotchas: The measured numbers depend on the suite's GambitC-prelude.scm, which adds (declare (standard-bindings) (extended-bindings) (block)); Gambit's defaults are (not standard-bindings) and (not extended-bindings), so plain code without these declarations will not inline primitives and will be slower. Safe mode was kept; (not safe) and (fixnum) are faster still but change semantics.

Harness and version sensitivity: one run per benchmark (NB_RUNS=1) on an Intel i3-N305; the suite first ran a v4.9.5-78 Gambit on 2026-01-16 (after switching the default from 'gambitc' to 'gsc', and Arch renames gsc to gambitc because of a Ghostscript clash), then re-ran v4.9.7 on 2026-02-03; v4.9.7 was about 1.11x faster by geomean than the earlier build, up to 4.3x on fft and 2.5x on mbrot (derived from the two results.GambitC revisions). The current release v4.9.8 (2026-08-09) is unmeasured.

Performance depends heavily on configure options: README recommends --enable-single-host --enable-march=native --enable-dynamic-clib for best performance, and INSTALL.txt calls --enable-single-host 'highly recommended' (about 2x interpreter speed), so a plain ./configure build will be slower than the Arch package used in the suite (the archived 4.9.4 PKGBUILD and the 4.9.5 options quoted in issue #854 both use --enable-single-host and --enable-gcc-opts; the 4.9.7 PKGBUILD could not be fetched).
Open performance anomaly issue #422 (2019): ##unchecked-structure-ref measured about 7x slower than the checked ##direct-structure-ref in an indirect-call loop.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Gambit over Bigloo or Loko when you want the fastest of the three on general Scheme code: in the same all.csv Gambit is about 1.28x faster than Bigloo 4.6a and 1.22x faster than Loko 0.12.1 by geomean (derived from page data), plus it has a C embedding story and a JS target; pick Chez Scheme (already catalogued) instead when GC-heavy or continuation-heavy throughput matters more than C output.
verified_claims_summary: ecraven/r7rs-benchmarks (about 55 Larceny/Gabriel programs, one run each, Intel Core i3-N305, Arch Linux packages): Gambit v4.9.7 executables built with 'gsc -o <out> -exe' in safe mode beat Guile 3.0.11 (guild compile -O3) on 45 of 53 shared rows, geomean 1.95x (1.78x excluding the call/cc rows ctak, fibc and cpstak), while Chez 10.3.0 is about 1.26x faster than Gambit overall; all ratios derived from all.csv.
